steps: Give it a minute — mail is rarely instant.

stepBackWhat.DRAFT: The join code stops working, so nobody new can ask for a seat. Everyone already at the table stays.
stepBackWhat.OPEN: The door reopens: anyone holding the code can ask for a seat again.
stepBackWhat.LOCKED: The pairings stay exactly as they are — they are not thrown away. Chefs simply cannot write their recipe again until you move forward.
stepBackWhat.ASSIGNED: Recipes become editable again, and the cooks stop seeing the one they received until you move forward. Anything already submitted stays submitted.
stepBackWhat.BRIEFS_CLOSED: The dinner stops being marked as happening. The recipes stay readable to the chefs cooking them.
stepBackWhat.DINNER: Voting closes. Ballots already cast are kept, and voting picks up where it left off if you move forward again.
stepBackWhat.VOTING: The results go back to provisional and are recalculated when you move forward. Every ballot is kept.

settings.stepBackNothingLost: Nothing is deleted by stepping back — only what people are allowed to do right now changes.

pass.title: The pass
pass.explain: The pass is the counter a kitchen calls orders across — everything goes through one person. Yours works the same way: it only ever shows what the dinner is waiting on you for right now, and it opens by itself when the evening is stuck on you. Nothing else lives here, so an empty pass means there is nothing to do.

lateJoin.title: Adding somebody now
lateJoin.short: Sign-ups are closed, so the code will be refused. Here is the way in.
steps: Step the dinner back to "Registration open".
Let the new chef join with the code.
On the chain page, use "Add to the chain" to fit them in.
lateJoin.keeps: Nothing is deleted. Every recipe already written and every message already sent is kept, and comes back the moment sign-ups close again.
lateJoin.pauses: While the door is open, chefs cannot write or read recipes. That resumes as soon as you move forward.
lateJoin.changes: Two things do change: if you chose specific courses, their number has to match the new number of chefs — and fitting the newcomer into the chain means one chef ends up cooking a different recipe than the one they had.

manual.title: Counting the hands
manual.chosen: This dinner votes by show of hands.
manual.howLead: Three rounds of hands. Suggested order: last place first.
howSteps: Before anything: everyone decides their own top three, silently. Deciding while the hands go up is how a table ends up voting for whatever the loudest person liked.
One hand per round, and never the same dish twice — you have one third place, one second and one first.
Not your own dish either. You know which one it is; everybody else is guessing.
Read the dishes out, ask who put each one in third place, count the hands and enter them. Then second, then first.
The app adds it up: third = 1 point, second = 2, first = 3.
manual.closeWhy: This writes these totals in as the dinner’s results and moves it on. The counts can no longer be changed.
manual.howManyHint: Count everyone at the table, not just the chefs — somebody who turned up without cooking still ate, and still gets a say.
manual.tooManyForDish: That is more hands than there are people. There are {{n}} voting.
manual.tooManyForPlace: That place has been given out {{n}} times already — everybody has exactly one to give.
manual.atTheTable: Counted at the table — raise your hand when the Executive Chef asks

pro.title: About Pro
pro.freeForever: The whole app stays free. Every dinner, every number of guests, every feature that changes how the game is played — the point is that everyone can do everything.
pro.what: Pro only sells flavour: better-looking tables, themed evenings (a Christmas one, a midsummer one), and — an idea still being worked out — letting a host share what they have bought with the guests at their table.

sections.heading: Who you are agreeing with
body: CovertCook is operated by Opus35 (opus35.fr). Writing to contact@opus35.fr reaches a person.
Using the app means accepting what is written here. If you do not accept it, do not use the app — there is no version of this where you are bound by something you never saw.

sections.heading: What the app is for
body: CovertCook organises a dinner where each guest secretly writes a recipe for another guest to cook. That is the whole product. It is not a marketplace, it handles no payments between guests, and it does not deliver food.
You need an account, and you must be old enough to hold one where you live — 15 in France, 16 in much of the EU, 13 in the UK and the US.

sections.heading: What you agree not to do
body: Do not use CovertCook to harass anybody, to send anything unlawful, or to get around the anonymity the game is built on. Trying to work out who wrote for whom before the reveal spoils the only thing the app is protecting.
Do not write a recipe you know somebody at that table cannot safely eat. The dietary panel exists so this is knowable; ignoring it is the one thing here that can actually hurt somebody.
The Executive Chef of a dinner can remove anybody from it. We can suspend an account used to harm people, and we will say why.

sections.heading: Your content
body: Your recipes, messages and dinner names stay yours. You give us only what is needed to run the app: storing them, showing them to the people in your dinner, and backing them up.
Delete your account and that content goes with it, except where removing it would break a dinner somebody else organised. What remains is then stripped of anything identifying you.

sections.heading: Free, and paid
body: Every part of the game is free and stays free: unlimited dinners, any number of guests, every feature that changes how the game is played.

A paid tier is planned for appearance only — tablecloths, themed evenings. Nothing is on sale yet. When it is, EU VAT rules and a statutory right of withdrawal apply, and these terms will say exactly how before anything is charged.

sections.heading: No promises we cannot keep
body: The app is provided as it is. We do not promise it will be available at a particular moment, that a dinner will go well, or that nobody will guess who wrote their recipe.
We are liable for what the law makes us liable for and no less — but not for a burnt dish, a guest who does not turn up, or an evening that did not go the way you hoped.

sections.heading: Changes, and the law that applies
body: If these terms change in a way that matters, the app will say so rather than updating a date quietly.
French law applies. If you are a consumer this does not remove the protections of the law where you live, and you keep the right to bring a dispute before the courts there.

sections.heading: Who holds your data
body: Opus35 (opus35.fr) is the data controller. contact@opus35.fr reaches a person, and questions about your data are answered there.

sections.heading: What is collected, and why
body: Your email address and password, to have an account at all. The password is never visible to us — it is hashed by our authentication provider.
A display name, which is what people who invite you see.
Your dietary restrictions, so that a dinner does not serve you something you cannot eat.
What you write in the app: recipes, the canned messages you send, the phrases you post to the fridge, and how you voted.
Nothing is collected for advertising. There is no advertising, no tracking across other sites, and no analytics profile of you.

sections.heading: Health data, said plainly
body: A severe allergy is health data. Under Article 9 of the GDPR that is a special category, and it is the most sensitive thing this app holds.

We ask for it because a dinner where nobody knows is genuinely dangerous, and we process it on the basis of your explicit consent — you type it in yourself, and you can remove it at any time from your profile.
It is shown to the people in your dinners as a list of restrictions with no name attached, so a cook knows what to avoid without knowing whose allergy it is.

sections.heading: Who else touches it
body: Supabase hosts the database and the accounts. Netlify serves the app. Cloudflare Turnstile checks that a sign-up comes from a person, and sees only what it needs to answer that. Resend sends email.
Each is a processor acting on our instructions. Nothing is sold, and nothing is shared with anybody not needed to make the app work.

sections.heading: How long it is kept
body: Your account and its content are kept while the account exists.
Fridge messages are deleted after 24 hours — they are small talk for one evening and worth nothing after it.
Delete your account and the rest goes with it, except where removing it would break a dinner somebody else organised; what stays is stripped of anything identifying you.

sections.heading: What you can ask for
body: Access to what we hold, correction of what is wrong, deletion, a copy in a portable form, and the right to object to processing or withdraw consent. For the dietary data, withdrawing consent means deleting it, which you can do yourself.
Write to contact@opus35.fr. If the answer does not satisfy you, you can complain to the CNIL in France, or to your own country's data protection authority.

sections.heading: Cookies
body: CovertCook stores a session token so you stay signed in, and your language choice. Both are necessary for the app to work, neither follows you anywhere, and there are no advertising or analytics cookies.
